maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: For a return showing during the seasons 1904, 1905, 1906, 1907, 1908, 1909 and 1910, wlxat amounts were paid to Messrs. Dussault & Lemieux, dredging contractors, for work done by the ' International,' the government dredge, leased to the said contractors.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext:
Would my hon. friend consent to adding the words ' so far as can be ascertained ' after the words ' dredging contractors.' The reason is this: during the early years of Dussault & Co's contract, which was awarded before I became minister, the dredge ' International ' was leased to the contractors, and the contractors paid a certain amount per cubic yard. Later on

-I do not remember in what year, but it was after I became a minister-instead of allowing so much per cubic yard, the dredging contractors were charged so much per day for the use of the dredge ' International.' My hon. friend can see that after that contract was made it would be, I assume, quite impossible to tell how much dredging was actually done by the * International,' because the services of the dredge were being paid for by the day. I may state, also, that the contractor had some three dredges of his own at work on the same dredging as that on which the ' International ' was engaged. If the hon. gentleman will consent -to the words ' so far as the same can be ascertained ' being added to the motion, I shall obtain all the information it is possible to obtain.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: Of course I cannot expect to get any more information than can possibly be ascertained, but it strikes me that it is easy to tell exactly the amount of dredging that would be done by the ' International.' There ought to be no difficulty in ascertaining that.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext:
The actual quantity taken away in the scows would be known, but whether it could be ascertained how much would be dredged by each dredge I do not know. If that can be ascertained it will be, and meantime I will ask my hon. Mend to consent to these words being inserted.

speechtext: ["In the old Bill, clause 8 provided that the man working eight hours should get the per diem wages, that is, the wages for ten hours' work. _ I think that is the intention of the Bill, From the present Bill that clause has been eliminated, so that if a man goes to a contractor to get work, the contractor will say to him: 'You do not have to work more than eight hours a day unless you like; you may if you choose work 10 hours; I am paying three dollars a day to those who work 10 hours.' If the man does not choose to work 10 hours a day, he gets no work on that contract. I want to know from the minister what follows. Suppose $3 is the regular 10 hr. current wages. If a man works only eight hours a day, the contractor has a right to pay the man only $2.40 a day, or a deduction of 2 hours. There is nothing in this Bill to make him pay more, unless the provision at the end of the Bill for one-fourth more than regular pay for overtime. It is intended to make the working man believe that this measure is in his favour, but it is not so unless it is distinctly provided that if he works eight hours he will get 10 hours' pay.\nProgress reported."]

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to ask the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) if anything is going to be done with respect to the preservation of the fish in the waters of the Trent river. I may say that dams have been erected along the Trent Valley canal without providing for a fish sluiceway. The waters of the Trent river have been noted for many years, at least as long as I can remember, for their beautiful game fish. Persons come in large numbers annually, especially from the Mr. MACLEAN (York).
United States, to fish in these waters, and leave a large amount of money with the people who live along the banks of the river. The view of many fishermen there is that the fish will follow the current and pass down through the locks and the basins until they reach the Bay of Quinte and Lake Ontario, whereas, if sluiceways were provided the fish would be turned back to their feeding grounds. Therefore, something should be done for the preservation of the fish of the waters of the Trent river.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: PRESERVATION OF FISH IN TRENT RIVER.
speechtext: In reply to the question raised by the hon. member for East Northumberland (Mr. Owen), it is one worthy of attention, and I will certainly make inquiry into the matter to see what the necessities are and what is being done in that connection.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I intended to have brought to the attention of the Hcuse an article which appeared in the ' Grain-Growers' Guide ' before the adjournment previous to the holidays, but owing to the rush which always exists on the day of the adjournment, I did not have an opportunity. The article I refer to is as follows:-

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).

speechtext:
The arrival of the farmers at Ottawa on December 16 is being awaited with intense interest by the members of the House. The fact that 40,000 Canadian farmers deem it worth while to send seven hundred delegates to Ottawa at the cost of $50,000 commands serious consideration. It comes home to the members of the House of Commons that if they had. been doing their duty as legislators the farmers' delegation would not have gone to Ottawa. There is no other construction to put upon the movement. Representative government at Ottawa has proved a decided failure. The western farmers have elected men to represent them and to protect their interests in the House of Commons, only to be laughed at and ignored by their members when election day is past. If the western members of the House of Commons were not absolutely false to the trust reposed in them the present situation would not have arisen. The western members know full well what the western farmers want, and they also know that the farmers represent a large majority of the western people. No person can doubt the justice of the farmers' demands, and yet their representatives have ignored them. There is not a single member in the House of Commons who has publicly expressed Ins belief in the justice of the organized farmers demands. This seems incredible yet it is true. Are the farmers too radical? Iliey were not too radical when they elected those gentlemen to Ottawa. If the western members stood together to protect the interests of their constituents they could force the hands of any government. To the ordinary member of the House of Commons the ' good of the

party5 comes first, while the people in the country care not about party so long as they get a square deal. The organized farmers should not go to the great expense and pains of presenting their case at Ottawa unless they do it in clear and unmistakable terms. It is time to read the ' Riot Act' to some of the misrepresentatives at Ottawa. They should be given to understand that their tenure of office is short unless their methods change. In western Canada every man favours government ownership and operation of the Hudson's Bay railway and the terminal elevators, and yet some of our members and also members of the government tell us that they (personally) ' do not believe in the principle of government ownership.' With all due respect to these gentlemen, they should be most clearly informed that it is the will of the people, and not of two or three men, that are supposed to prevail in British dominions. If the members of parliament and government are not prepared to obey the will of the people then it is time they gave way to men who are true democrats. The organized farmers have nothing to gain by undue humility to the members of the House of Commons or the government. They have right on their side and sooner or later there comes a day of reckoning for all those who openly and insolently refuse to regard the voice of the people.
I do not know what purpose the writer of this article had, because he certainly has ignored the facts. He may have had an ulterior motive, but I wish to tell the Grain Growers' Guide, or the person who wrote that article, that if he had been familiar with what has taken place in this House for many years back he certainly would not have misrepresented hon. members of this House. If he had taken the trouble to go back to 1903, he would have found at page 12626 of ' Hansard ' where my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) outlined the policy of the government ownership of terminal elevators, argued for it. He would also find that the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Sehaffner) brought up the question of a reduction in the tariff, and dividel the House upon it. He would also find that the same hon. member (Mr. Sehaffner) moved a resolution which was supported by every member from the west on this side of the House, on the question of government ownership of terminal elevators. Again, he would have found that when the Manitoba Grain Act was being amended, the Conservative members from the west asked the government to take hold of the terminal elevators in the very manner that these delegates recommended. He wonld also have found that the cold storage system had been many times discussed in this House and that recently a resolution moved from this side of the House in connection with the matter was I regret to say voted down. Then, the Hudson Bay railway is an old story, and if the writer of the -article had taken the trouble he would have found that the Conservative members of 48
the House had supported the very policy that the farmers of the west are agitating for. He would have found further that I myself moved a resolution in this House stating that the vacancy on the railway board should be filled by a practical farmer, and although that resolution was supported by the western Conservative members it was not adopted by the government. We have every right to ask the person who wrote that article to retract it; nay more, Mr. Speaker, I think we might go as far as you went on one occasion in this House and ask for an apology.

speechtext: I wish to ask the Prime Minister whether he has any further information to give to the House as to the negotiations with the government of the United States in regard to trade relations between the two countries, which are said to be now taking place at Washington, and whether, we are to have any information before the conclusion of these negotiations as to the basis upon which they are to proceed, and as to the principles upon which this government proposes to act, and finally, why is it that the right hon. gentleman has changed his mind as to going to Washington?	-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: TRADE NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: My hon. friend knows that at present there are _ commissioners of this government negotiating with commissioners appointed by the President of the United States with a view, if possible, to frame better trade relations between Canada and the United States; whether by treaty or otherwise will depend upon the negotiations. As to the basis upon which these negotiations are carried on, I do not know that I can add any information to that which the House is already in possession of. As to what will follow, the government will have to be judged by their action. Any treaty, or any policy which may be devised, if there be any, will be subject to the ratification of this parliament, my hon. friend included. As to my personal and oft repeated statement that we will have no further pilgrimages to Washington, I may say to my hon. friend that we have received an invitation which we acted upon, and we are prepared if possible to improve our trade relations with every nation, including our neighbours to the south.

I am not in any way wedded to the wording, but I showed the present wording to one of the most eminent lawyers in the House and he thought it was perfectly plain. If it will suit the member for Lincoln better I would suggest that lines 7, 8 and 9 be stricken out and the following substituted:
Whenever any principal money, interest, or other money secured by mortgage paid after the passing of this Act or by mortgage renewed by renewal extension agreement after the passing of this Act, is not paid at the time, &c.
I also submitted this form to the legal gentleman in question and he said that nothing could be plainer.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: You are using the words ' extension agreement ' as if some special legal construction should be given to them. I do not think any lawyer can say what the courts will hold an extension agreement is. The term ' extension agreement ' has no express significance that I know of, and it would require an interpretation clause to explain it. The courts may hold that an extension agreement is not necessarily what we have in our minds, they will put the ordinary construction upon the language. Why does not the hon. gentleman say ' an agreement extending the time for payments '. i think we should define with more precision what an ' extension agreement ' is.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: I am quite willing to adopt the suggestion of the hon. gentleman. I used the words ' extension agreement ' because I think they can be easily understood. If it will please the hon. member better to say, an agreement to extend the time for payment, I will be quite satisfied.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext:
I do not want the hon. gentleman to suggest that he is doing this to please me. He should not propose any legislation to please me or to please Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
the Prime Minister or any body else. If it is sensible legislation it should be passed by the House whether it pleases me or not, but we should be careful to word it so that it will be interpreted by the courts to mean what we intend. His suggested amendment still contains the words ' by a new mortgage or an extension agreement '. Why would not the hon. gentleman say ' or any agreement extending the time for the payment of the principal or the balance thereof as originally invested,' or something of that kind? The hon. gentleman, who is not a lawyer, may not know that there are such things as tacking securities, a man having two or three mortgages made by the same party to himself, or perhaps assigned to him by some other person and these in most provinces can be attached together and become practically one security. If the hon. gentleman means an agreement extending the time for payment of part of the original money I see no objection to that.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has taken up a good deal of time and has not allowed me to explain my position. I thought if I adopted that form of expression it would please my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) and would of necessity be sensible legislation that would be satisfactory to every one.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: This is the first time the hon. gentleman said that. If he had said it ten minutes ago he would have saved time.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: The hon. gentleman did not give me an opportunity.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: You wanted to becloud the matter.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: With all respect to my hon. friend I do not think this language can be improved, I think there can be no other meaning to the expression ' extension agreement ' than an agreement to extend. In ordinary English it cannot mean anything else than an agreement to extend the time for payment.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: Of what?

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: Of the moneys secured by the mortgage? However, if the hon. gentleman does not like that form of language we may allow it to stand, and I shall submit to him a form of expression of which he will approve.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext:
I understand the promoter of this Bill (Mr. Miller) said some time ago that there was an absolutely similar law in Ontario except that the time there was longer than the time intended to be prescribed here, that it is there six months instead of three. When this Act comes before the courts which law will prevail, the Ontario law or this Bill? Furthermore, as far as the principle of the Bill

goes, I am not in sympathy -with it. It may be that our control over interest or usury gives us some authority, tout this is nothing more than a civil contract where there is a penal clause on the party not living up to the contract, and I think that such legislation ought not to be supported by any lawyer in this House, especi-, ally those from Quebec who understand the regulation of contracts between parties under our Civil Code. The matter is without the jurisdiction of this parliament. The title given to the Bill will not change its purport and consequence and therefore I for one shall not support it.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: This Bill seems to me to toe quite in harmony with an Act passed by this House some years ago in regard to mortgages for more than five years. It is quite true that in regard to these this House could not authorize the payment off of a mortgage which was not due until the expiry of ten years, but, as I recollect, the House passed an Act, by virtue of the jurisdiction which this House has over interest, providing that if the amount is paid at the end of five years, no further interest shall be paid. This House could not say that the debt should be discharged or that the mortgage should be discharged but by reason of its jurisdiction over interest it could say, as the judgment of the House was at that time, that thereafter no further interest should be paid. The present Bill seems to me entirely analogous. It simply says that in certain extents no interest shall be collected. My experience leads me to believe that this is in the interests of the general public. My experience has been mostly with borrowers and I have known many cases of hardship. Farmers are not so punctilious as business men, many of them are not awake to the fact that they have to pay a bonus of three months' interest before they are allowed to pay off their mortgage. It may be said that the paying off of a mortgage at any time may disarrange the business of the loan companies, but the inconvenience and disarrangement of their business is not great as they are constantly getting in and lending out money. Certainly the inconvenience to them is insignificant compared with the hardship on a poor farmer or man who mortgages his home in a town, who is struggling to pay off a mortgage and finds that he has to' pay interest for two or three months for which he receives no return.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: Is it a penal clause?

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext:
It is a penal clause if he does not pay the interest on the day it is due. Sometimes a mail goes astray, perhaps a man is arranging to get another loan and they take advantage of "that and he has to pay the additional interest. That is a great hardship and it seems to me should not be tolerated.
Whether or not the words ' extension agreement ' are the best words that could be used it seems to me it cannot make any practical difference and cannot cause any confusion because the only effect which that has is in regard to the time when the mortgage is given. If the mortgage is made after the passing of this Act the law applies. It does not seem to me there can be very much doubt about the meaning of the words and I should think the present wording is as good as could be chosen.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: I agree with the' hon. Solicitor General (Mr. Bureau). I do not believe that the Bill is one over which we have jurisdiction. According to the British North America Act, matters regarding civil rights are decided exclusively by the provincial legislatures. We in Quebec have _ no sympathy at all with this kind of legislation. I have discussed the proposition with several lawyers of the Montreal bar and every one of them has declared himself against it. Upon principle I should say that we should oppose this Bill. The hon. member has referred to legislation of a similar character which was passed by this parliament some years ago. Even if that was done I do not believe that is a good reason why we should do the same thing to-day. If I had been a member of the House at the time I should not only have voted against the Bill but should have opposed it to the fullest extent. We in Quebec, and in this, I think we are like the people of every other province, are jealous of our provincial rights, and this is a matter to be dealt with only toy the legislatures. I do not believe that it will affect us very much in our province. When a mortgage is due the debtor has a perfect right to pay at any time by paying tire interest which has been agreed upon in the deed, but of course under this Bill it is stated that after the mortgage is due the debtor will have no right to pay the mortgage, that he is bound to keep it upon his farm or his house for a longer period, that he is not at liberty to pay it off. In our province we are not confronted with that state of affairs.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: What is the law in your province if the mortgage is not paid on the day it is due?

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext:
Unless there is a clause in the deed which must be construed, as the Solicitor General says, as a penal clause, the debtor is at perfect liberty to pay off the mortgage at any time by simply jjaying the accrued interest from the time the mortgage is due until the day he pays it off. Such being the case, I say there is no justification for this parliament to obtain an end by invalid means which cannot be obtained in a direct manner. I think every legal mind will agree that we have no right to interfere with private contracts, contracts

that are made between individuals. Now, if we do interfere therewith, even though m an indirect way, we do that which we have no right to do. Since the principle is admitted that this is a matter under the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures, T say we should not pass this kind of legislation. It is a bad principle, it is bad legislation, and we should leave the whole matter to be decided by the provincial legislatures. As a member of the bar of the province of Quebec, I should have to vote against that amendment.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: I am afraid the hon. member for Montreal has not read this amendment, perhaps, as carefully as he should have done. No hon. gentleman in this House will disagree with him when he states that questions of contract are within the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures, and we have no right to interfere with them. But he forgets that by the British North America Act questions of interest are purely within the jurisdiction of this House. All that this Bill seeks to do is to provide that after a mortgage becomes due, if the mortgagee will not take his money, then the mortgagor can give him one month's notice, agreeing to pay one month's interest, and the mortgagee must accept- his money.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: After it is past due?

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext:
Certainly. Now, I can tell my hon. friend that in the province of New Brunswick I have known case after case where a man failed to pay his mortgage after it was due, he has gone later on to the mortgagee with the money, and the mortgagee says: No, I wont accept it. I do not want to particularize, but I can tell him that a man who occupied a very high position in the judiciary of New Brunswick within the last five or six years, in a case in which I was personally interested, re- fused to accept the money because the money was not paid the day it -was due, and the parties were compelled to pay interest for seven or eight months on an amount of four or five thousand dollars, simply because they had no right to compel that man to take his money until the next year came round. That may seem a remarkable statement, but I am giving an actual fact that occurred in my own practice. It seems to me it is only reasonable that the mortgagor should have the right to go to the mortgagee and say: Here is a month's interest,* I want you to take your money. Now, we are not asking the mortgagee to discharge the mortgage; we admit that this House has no jurisdiction to say to the mortgagee that he should discharge the mortgage, because that is made as a civil contract. All this Bill says is: If you do not take your money, then you cannot get interest after one month. The British Mr. RIVET
North America Act has placed the question of interest within the jurisdiction of this parliament, and therefore I submit that we have a perfect right to pass this legislation, and say to a man: If you wont take your money when it is [DOT] due, along with one month's interest, you cannot claim any more interest. I am not saying that he must discharge the mortgage, as that is a matter within the jurisdiction of the local legislature. It seems to me that no argument can be advanced why this Bill should not become law.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext:
There seems to be some doubt whether this House has jurisdiction to deal with this matter; but if it has, 1 quite agree with those hon. gentlemen who think that it ought to be exercised. The one fault that I have with this proposed amendment is that it does not go far enough. I do not see any ground, on principle, why a mortgagor should pay one month's interest. I think the matter should be simplified by giving him the right to pay whenever it becomes due, or at any time thereafter. Why should he pay interest for a month after he becomes prepared to repay the loan? I am quite satisfied that every lawyer in this House has in his practice met cases such as my hon. friend from Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Carvel), has referred to. I do not think that in private mortgages there is so much difficulty; but in case of many mortgage corporations a long printed form is used, three large pages, the mortgagor often does not read his mortgage. He is told in nine cases out of ten: I won't take up the time to read these three pages of fine print, it is a formal matter, and the mortgagor signs his mortgage. It is provided in the mortgage that if he does not pay on the very day when it becomes due he should pay a bonus of three months' interest, but that provision has not been read to him at all, in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred he does not know it is there. He signs the mortgage, it is sent away, it is registered, final search is made, and he does net get his money perhaps for ten days after he has signed the mortgage. He knows that the mortgage has to run for five years, and he dates it in his mind from the day when he gets the money. He perhaps signs the mortgage on the first day of the month, but does not get his cheque for the loan until perhaps the tenth of the month. He has it in his mind that five years from that tenth of the month his mortgage will become due. On that tenth of the month five years hence he comes to pay his money, and he is told: Why, this money wras due on the first of the month. But I did not get the money until the tenth. I don't know anything about that, but here is a provision in the mortgage that you agreed to, that if it is not paid on the exact day when it becomes due, you will pay a bonus of three months' interest.

Then for the first time he discovers there is a provision of that kind in the mortgage. Now it may be said, as it has been said, that it is not wise to interfere with private contracts. But instances have been cited where that has been done, it seems to me that in the interest of the public we are quite justified in doing so in certain cases, and I believe this is one of those cases. Where is there any hardship upon the mortgagee in requiring him to take the money on the second day of January, or on the 5lh day of January, as well as on the 1st, so long as he gets interest on the money up to the date on which it is paid? There is no such provision in regard to any other securities. You give your promissory note for $1,000, payable, say, in one, or two, or three months. If it is not paid the exact day it becomes due, you have a right to pay it the next day, or ten days afterwards. You simply pay interest for the time you have the money. And where does the hardship come in upon the mortgagee in requiring him to take the money at any time after it becomes due? If he lvants it all upon the day it becomes due and has another investment for it, he should do as the manager of a bank does, notify his debtor that the money will be due on a certain day. If the mortgagee wants his money on the exact day, he can simply notify the mortgagor a week or ten days before, saying: That money is due on a certain day, and I want it on that day, because I have another investment in view. It seems to me that, instead of saying as this Bill does, that if he does not pay at the end of the month, he will have to pay the bonus provided for in the mortgage, the whole matter ought to be simplified by merely giving the mortgagor a right to pay the money at any time after it becomes due, notwithstanding any provision in the mortgage to the contrary. Although a man may agree to let his money stand on a certain mortgage for ten years, this House, in its_ wisdom, has already said that it is in the interest of the public that the mortgagor should have the right to pay it off at the expiration of five years. Of course, this is interfering with private contract. There are many cases where we have done that. It is a question [DOT]of expediency whether in actual life it is not in the interest of the public to say that a mortgagor should have the right to pay a mortgoge' after it comes due by giving one, two or three months' notice, or without any notice whatever. I intended to move an amendment to that .effect. I did not know the Bill was coming up to-day, but if my hon. friend will allow this matteT to stand, I will have an opportunity of giving notice of the amendment that I desire to move that the mortgagor shall have the right to pay at any time after it comes due.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: There is no necessity of notice for that.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: Does my hon. friend think that under the provisions of the Bill as it stands now there is any hardship to the borrower in having to give a month's notice?

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: Is there any reason why he should give the notice or, if he does not pay the mortgage on the exact day that it falls due he should be deprived of the opportunity of paying it?

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: I think there is. It is not on behalf of the loan companies that I take this position because loan companies are in a position to protect themselves. The money comes in and goes out almost as a matter of routine, but, to the small lender of money I think it would be only fair to say that he should at least- have a month's notice after the money or the mortgage becomes due and when he is required to look about for a reinvestment. It is often the case that some considerable time is lost in reinvesting money. It is not always easy to pick out investments. It appears to me that it is only fair to a small lender of money that, if a mortgage becomes overdue and the money is not paid, he should receive at least a month's notice, that the borrower, who has not lived up to his contract by paying when the money became due should, in justice to the lender, give him a month's notice so that he may reinvest his money. I do not think that involves any hardship to the borrower and I think it is only simple justice to the lender of the money.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: As to the desire of the mortgagor to make payment before the whole mortgage becomes due I admit there is a good deal in what the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) says. But this is not dealing with a matter of that kind. We all know that in mortgages there is often a provision that the mortgagor shall have the privilege of paying a certain portion of the principal sum or any part of it before the whole amount thereof becomes due. I could understand that if the mortgagee were not expecting the money to come in the case might be different, but he should expect it to come in when it is due at the end of the mortgage period, or at the end of the year, and if he wants it particularly at that time for some other investment it is no hardship on him to give notice to the mortgagor that he wants his money on a particular day. At the present time when the rate of interest has been going down-

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: (York) It has been going up.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: -my experience is that the mortgagee is very glad to have the mortgagor hold the money for six or twelve months because, although there may be a little difference at the present time, the tendency of the rate of interest is downward.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: Not of late.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: I say not of late.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Crothers) was pretty logical in the argument he made this afternoon, but I want to call his attention to a little different state of facts than that which he has in mind. If a mortgagor came in five or ten days after the mortgage was due and wanted to pay the money I think the mortgagee should accept it. But, let us suppose that it should go over for nine months, the mortgagee would not reasonably be expecting the mortgagor to come in and pay the money. Does my hon. friend not think that in a case like that the mortgagee should have at least cne month's time to enable him to reinvest? It looks to me as if the Bill drafted by my hon. friend from South Grey (Mr. Miller) more fairly meets all the conditions that may arise in the lending of money than if you *were to undertake to say that he must take the money and discharge the mortgage so that the mortgagor cannot pay any interest from that time.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: Does not my hon. friend think that if the mortgagee wants the money before the mortgagor comes in it is simply a matter of telling him so?

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext:
I think the Bill is perhaps a little more reasonable and fair to all parties as it stands now. It may be that a man has money borrowed from his neighbour and his mortgage will mature on the first February, 1911; that man may go to his neighbour and say: I will not have this money on the first February, but I will have it shortly afterwards and I will be glad if you will allow it to stand. In that case the mortgagee is allowing his money to remain out to accommodate the man to whom he has loaned money, and I think it is not unfair that the man who has loaned the money should have one month's notice in order to find a new investment. The hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Crothers) expressed in the first words that lie uttered with respect to this Bill some little doubt as to our jurisdiction. The words he used were somewhat as follows,
' If this House has jurisdiction.' If there is any doubt in the mind of any hon. member as to the jurisdiction of this House to pass the Bill that doubt must be removed by looking at section 10 of the Interest Act, the same chapter that this Bill seeks to amend. That section 10 was introduced by the Hon. Edward Blake more than thirty years ago, and the Bill that I have before the committee now is a copy in as far as can be of section 10 introduced by Mr. Blake, and certainly if the House had jurisdiction in that case it has jurisdiction in this. Again, if we had the right to interfere with the I Mr. CROTHERS.
right of contract when section 10 was introduced we have the same right to-day and this Bill does no more to violate that right than does section 10. In many other cases and by a great deal of other legislation we have interfered with the right of contract. For instance, in our Ontario statutes we say that a mechanic who furnishes labour, or a man who furnishes material for work, notwithstanding that he may have signed an agreement not to place a mechanic's lien, cannot waive his right under any agreement which he may sign for the supplying of the material or- the doing of the labour. Not many weeks ago the House accepted the principle of this Bill by a very large vote and it seems to me that now is hardly the time or the place to undertake to argue against the principle of the Bill. One of the hon. members for the province of Quebec has argued against the Bill and he has said that the members of the bar in Quebec are opposed to the Bill. But, in his remarks he also says that this Bill will not very much affect the people of Quebec. Therefore, if it does not have any harm in it and he only thinks it is without any good, it is not a very good reason why it should not become law. Section 10, introduced by Mr. Blake, has been of very great benefit to borrowers in the Dominion of Canada ever since it became law.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: I take very much the same view of this Bill as that held by my hon. friend (Mr. Crothers) regarding its legality.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: While my hon. friend (Mr. Macdouell) proceeds to argue in that way, will he kindly say co the committee why he thinks this Bill to be illegal or beyond our jurisdiction if section 10 of the Interest Act is legal?

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: Was section 10 of the Interest Act held to be legal by the courts?

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: It was never decided before the courts.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: Section 10 has been upon the statute-books for thirty years and if this statute was to the disadvantage of every loan company in Canada, and if these loan companies, with all their zeal to protect their rights have been injured and have had their rights curtailed, they have not seen fit to contest it or to argue that it is not legal.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext:
I was going to observe that it occurs to me that the Bill is entirely one of civil rights. _ It is clearly a matter within the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures and while not opposing the principle of the Bill I think the Bill should be dealt with, in and by the proper authority. I think it will be found upon analysis that the laws of the different provinces with regard to interest and mort-

gages and with regard to the matters treated of in this Bill are very much at variance. Each province has adopted laws best suited to itself. I understand that the law in the province of Ontario is quite the reverse of the law in the province of Quebec with regard to the right of the mortgagor to repay the mortgage money after the maturity of the security. That is a reason why the question should be dealt with as a local matter of civil rights coming within the purview of the province. My opinion is that this Bill, if passed, will not be an infra vires statute. Even if it is legal and if it is passed, I think the Bill will do more harm than good to the borrowers. The effect of this legislation would be that immediately the security matures the lender, whether he be a loan company or a private lender, will immediately insist upon getting his money, which might prove a great hardship to the borrower, or, he will at least insist on getting what is known as an extension agreement the cost of which will be from $10 to $15 according to the amount involved.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: These are city prices.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: No, I think there is a tariff which governs these matters throughout the province of Ontario.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: They put a lot of expense on the borrower for revaluation.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: Yes, they will put the borrower to the expense practically of a new loan. I do not believe that one-half of the loans are paid when they mature.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: In practice do they not have renewals?

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: No ; it is my experience, and I think the experience of most gentlemen who practise law in Ontario, that the borrower makes some kind of a verbal arrangement to pay the mortgage off in a year or six months, relying on the law as it stands regarding notice or the bonus that must be paid. If the borrower has the right to pay off at any time, the lender would say: I must know when my money is to come back, because I have to seek reinvestment, and in nine cases out of ten the borrower will be put to the expense of practically a new loan. In my opinion the Bill should not pass; first, because I do not think it is constitutional, and secondly, because I believe it will prove a hardship rather than a boon to those in whose interests it is supposed to be passed.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: When we passed the second reading of the Bill we adopted its principle and assumed responsibility for our jurisdiction. My legal experience leads me to believe that the Bill is admirably in the interest of the farming community, the small borrowers. We talk about not interfering with private contracts, but in these days of corporations and large aggregations of wealth there is no equality between the poor borrower and the wealthy loan company when they come to negotiate. Usually, the borrower swallows holus-bolus whatever is presented to him without reading the small print. I was surprised to hear the Solicitor General say that this law would not be applicable in the province of Quebec.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: I did not make any such statement.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: Perhaps it was the member for Hochelaga who said that. I know a gentleman who desired_ to negotiate a loan in Montreal in connection with property he had there, and a week before the loan matured he secured the promise of the loan company that they would grant the loan if the title was satisfactory, but the opinion of the lawyers on the title (which proved in the end to be satisfactory) was delayed for some two or three weeks, and so the loan was not paid off when it became due and the mortgagor was under penalty. I repeat that I am strongly in favour of the Bill.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman from Toronto (Mr. Macdonell) said that a renewal agreement would cost from $10 to $15, but I know of one large Ontario company which makes a practice of granting these renewals or extension agreements without any charge at all, and while there is one firm of solicitors in Toronto which does charge $5 for an extension agreement, most of the solicitors only charge three dollars. If a lender will by verbal agreement extend the time for payment without asking for a revaluation, it is absurd to think that he will insist on a valuation when there is and because there is a written agreement. I may say that since the Bill was first introduced I have never found one man, outside the House of Commons, -who was not interested in some way in loan companies, who opposed the Bill, and I have found a large number of farmers and others who were strongly in favour of it. I have spoken to some gentlemen from the city of Toronto who were at the heads of large money-lending institutions and who have told me that the Bill as presented was very reasonable. Two very prominent and eminent gentlemen engaged in lending money have made this statement to me, but as there is a difference of opinion among those at the head of lending institutions in Toronto concerning the Bill, I do not think it would be fair to mention their names. However, I may say that Mr. Osier, one of the members for Toronto, said to me last session-and I do not think it is any breach of confidence for me to mention it-that he

thought the Bill was not in any way unreasonable and that it would not do any harm to any person. When we adopted the second reading of the Bill we agreed to its. principle and I do not think it is now reasonable to introduce the question of our jurisdiction.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: I do not think that the hon. gentleman should insist so much on our having adopted the principle of the Bill, when we gave it its second reading merely to save timie and with the understanding that we would discuss all its features in committee. It is not to be understood that we are swallowing the principle of the Bill; otherwise, there will be a great deal of time occupied every session by hon. gentlemen explaining their position before they take the responsibility of not dividing the House on every public Bill, whether it comes from the government side or the opposition side of the House. I think my hon. friend should not try to take advantage of that technicality, if it can be dignified by that term. When we pass this Bill into Committee of the Whole, we cannot tell what principle is involved in it until we see what it will look like when we get through with it. If the Dominion has jurisdiction in this matter, the provinces also have jurisdiction, and I am inclined to think that it would be better to leave it wholly to the provinces. I do not say that as a matter of law the Dominion has not the power to pass this legislation, but the arguments presented as to the propriety or impropriety of passing it indicate to me that it is a local matter-that what might be fair in one province might be exceedingly unfair in another. Is the rate of interest to-day the same in Nova Scotia as in British Columbia, or the same in Alberta as in Ontario? It seems to me, in view of all these differences, that this matter had better be legislated upon By the provinces. My hon. friend from West Elgin, for whose opinion I have great respect, thinks the borrower should not be obliged to give any notice at all, and I think there is as much to be said in favour of that as in favour of a month's notice. That shows that there is a difference of opinion even in Ontario. Then, the lenders of money are not always corporations. Many farmers who have amassed a little money lend it to other farmers. Even if we have technically the power to pass this legislation, the provinces certainly have the power, and I would suggest that my hon. friend get the provincial government of Ontario to consider what he is doing. No one on either side of this House will say that the government of Sir James Whitney is not always ready to look after the interests of the ordinary people of the prov-

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
speechtext: ince. Then, hon. gentlemen from Quebec have given very good reasons why this legislation would not meet the approval of the people of - that province. It seems to me that the evil, if it does exist, is trivial, or at all events is such that any provincial government can take hold of and cure it for its own province. For all these reasons, I am inclined to think that the best interest of the country would be to leave the provincial legislatures to deal with the matter.

speechtext:
I wish to say a few words on this section. I am very much opposed to this Bill, not that it makes any difference to me what the hours of labour may be on a government work. But there is, and has been in the past a tendency among young men to leave the farms and Xlrift to the

towns and cities, and the usual excuse they make is that in towns and cities men only work eight or ten hours a day, while they have to work much longer on the farm. This Bill is an indirect injury to the farmers, because it will have the effect of making" young men on the farms more dissatisfied, and will increase their desire to go away to the towns and cities where they think they will have to work shorter hours.
I think that the law of demand and supply should be allowed to work freely, and we should not provide for legislation that certain men shall only work certain hours. I believe that any man who is willing to work ten hours and take his pay for ten hours, should have the right to do so. We have no right to say in this House that a man shall only work eight hours a day and draw pay for that time. I feel satisfied that any large contractor, in this city or anywhere else, if he knows that men can get work at eight hours a day, he will be willing to employ them eight hours, and pay them accordingly. He has a certain contract to do and he must have the work done. This Bill, if passed, as far as I can see, would be taking away the rights of any man who wants to work eleven or twelve hours. I do not think that is right. I believe that every man who has a family to support has the right to work as many hours as he wishes. I feel it is indirectly a great injury to the farmers and I will oppose it. I claim that this question should be left over until there are more members in the House. There are only half of them here to-day and they should have a chance to express their opinions upon this measuie.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).

There must be some reason-I have not heard it advanced yetr-as to why the day labourer working for the government shall be restricted to eight hours' work whilst the labourer working equally as hard and in the same grades of labour in any other work shall be at liberty to work nine, ten, twelve, or any hours that are conditioned by the contract. I have not heard a reason given why this should be so. Perhaps the Prime Minister can tell us what reason there is.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.

My object in putting that in is that the government are sometimes carrying out public _ works by day labour. If that were not in the Bill the men who are working for the government would be probably working nine or ten hours, while men working on contract would not if this Bill passes. If it is fair to ask parliament to pass a law providing that contractors shall be compelled to work
their men only eight hours a day, or forty-eight hours a week, or over time paid for at a certain rate, it is also fair for the government to do the same thing when they are doing work on public buildings by day labour. That is the reason. I do not see why the government, who are supposed to be model employers, from whom other employers should copy, should be exempt. The object is to put on exactly the same footing work under the day labour system and work under contractors.

I would like to point out, with regard to what my hon. friend from Haldimand (Mr. Lalor) has very properly mentioned, that apparently the promoter of this Bill does not realize quite what this Bill will do and what it will not do. There is a class of employees of the government-lock tenders and so on on the canals-'and I think they are working eleven and twelve hours a day. If I am not mistaken it is eleven or twelve hours, and I am pretty sure it is twelve hours. At all events, it is more than ten. Has the hon. gentleman no sympathy for these men? They are working for the government; they are not hired by the day, but they are hired, by the month. A man who happens to be hired by the day and at a much higher rate of wages has only to work eight hours a day. Is it these few preferred individuals who are to be worked only eight hours a day and receive the big wages of the mechanic, and is the poorer man, who works for the same government, to go on striving for twelve hours a day, because he is paid by the month instead of by the day? That is the effect of the Bill as it stands. Not being employed by the day, they will have Mr. MIDDLEBRO.
to keep on working as long as the government demands.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
If I rightly apprehend the tenor of the discussion upon this Bill to-day and on the previous occasion, the idea which underlies the Bill is not universally popular. A good many objections to the Bill have been stated. There is much to be said in favour of the view that, if the Bill comes into force, it should apply to all kinds of labour employed by the government. But, on the other hand, even hon. gentlemen who say that logically this Bill, if passed, should be made to apply thus extensively would not be prepared to vote for such legislation if it were offered to them. This legislation is tentative as I understand it. It is not, I believe, the result of long-settled conviction, but it has been urged upon the government again and again by workingmen's associations. It has been represented to us, and it is perfectly true, that in other countries legislation has been adopted of a character identical with this. The labour organizations have done a great deal during the last century, and especially during the last sixty years, for the advancement of the labouring classes. The time has passed when the labouring classes were treated as-slaves; they' are acknowledged now to be citizens. By a long series of Acts passed by different parliaments they have brought themselves to the proud position they occupy at this moment. Every one who has followed the labour movement throughout the world knows that in this and other countries there is a strong movement in favour of an eight hour day. In different countries, and, as I understand it, in Great Britain, a law exists at the present time which limits the day of labour to eight hours not for all classes of labour, not even for all classes of labour employed by the government, but for certain classes, and especially for what we may call contractual labour. The workingmen's associations, after due consideration, have urged the introduction of this legislation. It does not cover the whole field, far from it; it simply covers one part of the field, and it is intended to see how it would work, how it will affect men who work for the government, As an abstract proposition, if you say that one class of labourers should be compelled to work not more than eight hours a day, it is not easy to understand by what process of reasoning it is decided that the same law should not be applied to other classes of labour. But the answer is that there are some classes of labour in which it is impossible to limit the number of hours that a man may work. There are men in this House. I know, who work more than eight hours a day. There are many classes of men who work, ten, twelve, fourteen, sixteen hours a day, not every day,

perhaps, but most of the days of the year. It has been stated that the farmers work more than eight hours a day. True, we know that there are seasons when the farmer works fourteen to sixteen hours a day. But, on the other hand, there are seasons when they do not have to work even eight hours a day. For this class of labour, this Bill does not undertake to provide at all. This Bill provides only for that class of labour which I call contractual labour, labour for the government on public buildings carried on under contract or, in the absence of a contract, done by day labour. The Bill does not go beyond that, and, as I have just stated, it is tentative. I do not think that any one will say that this law will work with entire satisfaction, but it is a step, I believe, in the right direction. I understand that there are cities in Canada to-day, including Toronto and Montreal, where that which it is proposed to establish under this Bill already exists not only for government work, but for private work, that in these cities masons, carpenters, joiners and other workers have the benefit of the eight-hour day. That is done voluntarily, as a matter of contract and agreement between the employers and employees. The object of the Bill is to make this compulsory in the class of government labour to which it refers.. For my part, I would not propose to give the law a greater extension at this time, but I think it is well that we should, to this extent, yield to the request of the labour organizations which have repeatedly pressed this upon parliament. My hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) put a question a moment ago, but I think it was well answered by my hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Ver-ville). But I would observe that we have a law to-day under which a provision is inserted in every contract with the government that the contractor shall pay fair wages-the contractor must not squeeze his men, paying them only as little as their circumstances compel them to accept, but must pay a fair wage according to the locality in which the work is carried on. This Bill is in accordance with that principle. The labourer upon a government work will not be compelled to work more than eight hours a day, but, as I understand it, he will get eight hours' pay. If he works more, the law provides that he shall have extra remuneration.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
There seems to be a difference upon questions of fact as between the introducer of the Bill and the Prime Minister, and it seems to me that now is the proper time to have a fair understanding of what the Bill means. The hon. gentleman who introduced the Bill says that, in his oninion. the Bill applies to all classes of labour emoloyed by the government. The Prime Minister, if I understand him correctly, is of opinion that it applies only
to certain classes of mechanics working upon public buildings. In view of this difference of opinion, I think we should have it clearly understood what the Bill really does mean. For my part, I think that if we pass a measure of this kind it should apply equally to the labourer on the canals and other public works who are working for the government as well as to the high-priced mechanics working upon public buildings. If it applies to the mechanic who earns perhaps fifty cents an hour, it certainly should apply to the man working on the canals at small remuneration.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Lalor) will see that the man who works on the canal has steady employment and is willing to take, perhaps, a lower wage on that account. There are seasons of the year when men on the canals have to work ten or twelve hours a day and are glad to do so. But this steadiness of employment does not apply to the labour referred to in this Bill, which is only contractual labour.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: In my own constituency, where a branch of the Welland canal is located, the men employed on that work are not the class of men the Prime Minister has in view. They are men in continuous employment, working by the month. I *am speaking of the labouring man who is employed by the government from day to day on the public works of the country. I do not see why he should be overlooked or placed at a disadvantage as compared with other employees of the government.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: The hon. member knows that the hon. member who has introduced this Bill is proposing the adoption of a new principle by legislation, and he wisely proposes to limit its application at the outset in order to demonstrate how this new principle will operate. He believes that had he made the application of the Bill very much wider, it would have had verv little chance of passing through this parliament. If after the Bill is on the statute-book for some time, and hon. gentlemen opposite are willing to take the view they are now expressing, it will be quite possible to widen its scope. But to do that at the outset would be to ensure the defeat of the measure.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
I would like to see on what principle the Bill is founded. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister tried to make a distinction between casual labour and permanent labour; but is he consistent in that? Men employed on a public building are obliged to work only eight hours a day, while men employed for instance. on a bridge across the street, have not the same privilege. On what principle will the Prime Minister justify the govern-

ment in protecting the one set of m<Tn and not the other? Both are engaged in temporary employment, the one not more hazardous nor calling for more exertion than the other. What is the result of this discrimination? It immediately causes disquiet, unrest, a sense of injustice, and consequently agitation. This will not be a good thing for this country. But it goes still further than that. 1 think that we as members ought to discuss Uiis question whether we are in the sight of the labour organizations or not. What are we here for? We are here to do our best, in this legislation as in other, for- the country's interest. I know that men are asked by labour unions to support this legislation. I know that they are asked not to support it, in other interests. It is not for members to say, I will not put my views of this matter before the House because I might offend the one or the other. I think it is for us to see that this matter, if it is justified at all, is justified on principle. By what right shall the government, which exacts certain labour from a man for good pay, steady pay and sure pay, make his position easier than that of the man who works for another paymaster, may be not so good in any particular, and who does just as hard work? By this measure you not only cause a grievance to the man engaged in a certain employment as against another man working for the same paymaster, but the thing goes far wider than that. Alongside of the men working for the government, for good pay and sure pay, and working only eight hours a day, you have to consider the farmers of the country and the labouring men who work with them, who work often sixteen or eighteen hours a day, and whose average for the whole year will be far more than eight hours a day, for less or no greater pay.
Do you suppose that this does not raise discontent? Carpenters who are working on a government building only work eight hours a day ; carpenters who are not working for the government have to work longer ; there is a disability on the one as compared with the other and it must produce widespread discontent. So far as is possible no man should labour unduly, but every man has to earn his bread by the sweat of his ibrow and there are few working men who do not put in' more than eight hours per day. True, their wages are not more than they ought to get and in many cases they are not as much as they ought to get. There are some kinds of labour with regard to which the law should step in and make-the hours shorter because the labour is of such a nature that it wears out the physical or the mental life of the men who labour in these occupations. I need not mention the kind of work in which short lives are the absolute lot of Mr. FOSTER.
the men who engage in them, iat all events if they work many hours per day. In such cases, after broad inquiry and full information parliament should say that in the interests of the health of these citizens the hours per day during which they labour ought to^ be limited. But there is nothing of this kind in the government's plan, and I take it that it is the government's plan because the leader of the government is supporting the Bill. I am anxious to find out how far this Bill goes. It says :
Every contract hereafter made for the erection, remodelling, construction or repair of any building, to which the government of Canada is a party, which may involve the employment of labourers, workmen, or mechanics, shall contain a stipulation that no labourer, workman, or mechanic in the employ of the contractor, sub-contractor, or other person doing or contracting to do the whole or any pant of the work contemplated by the contract, &c.
Does not that go off from the building itself and does it not go out into the private factory and discriminate 'against the man who as a subcontractor is making a boiler for your public building, or a gas pipe, or electric fittings, or anything at all that goes into that building? How will it work out in a man's factory when he is engaged in general work of that kind, paying his men so much under contract. Here is a law which says that no man who is engaged in that work shall work more than eight hours a day. If that be so then you introduce disorder and confusion into the industries which are making what is contributory to the contractor's work.
