maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: I do not think my words would convey the impression that I meant to go as far as the Minister of Labour thought I did when he corrected me. I think that the wording of section 3, goes far enough to cause this same confusion and disorganization of whien 1 have spoken in the carrying out of public work. I would ask the mover of the Bill or the Minister of Labour or the Prime Minister on what principle they justify the exclusion of all -but workers upon a public building what just ground there is for doing that that will not cause discontent and show disparity?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
My hon. friend (Mr. Foster) stated in a very substantial way the Objection which exists to all such legislation. The answer is obvious, and my hon. friend has given it himself. He has said he would not object to legislation which would regulate certain kinds of labour, that there are certain kinds of labour that are dangerous in themselves, injurious to health, such as work in mines, and he said that he could conceive in such circumstances that the law might step in and regulate that kind of labour. In some countries it has been done, to some extent in this country. For instance, in England and most other countries there is legislation prohibiting labour by children or women. This only goes to show that it is not at all a thing absolute. It is quite convenient, nay it is legitimate that legislation should step in to regulate labour. Here legislation is stepping in to regulate labour. My hon. friend asks properly what is the principle on which you regulate this class of labour, and not any other class of labour. Labour has been organized for not more than 60 years at most in order to vindicate the rights of those who were labour-49
ers, and who prior to that time had been limited only by the will of their masters. Labour has been organized and labour organizations have constantly pursued for the last 50 or 60 years the betterment of the working classes. My hon. friend knows that one of the objects of labour organizations in all countries is to limit the hours of labour which simply concern these labour organizations. My hon. friend has said that farmers are not limited by any law and that they sometimes work from 14 to 18 hours a day. That is true, but every one knows that by custom, if not by legislation there is a great difference between the man who works as a plumber or a mason, and the man who works for a farmer. When the farmer hires help it is expected by both employer and employed that the employee will be called on to work longer at certain seasons than at others, but it is also known that by custom if not by law, all these classes of labour spoken of, the carpenter, the mason, the joiner, are expected to work only during a certain number of hours. That number varies, it is sometimes eight hours, or nine hours, or ten hours. From time immemorial my hon. friend has only to recall his own experience when he was a child and I was a child to recognize that work on buildings has been carried on from certain hours to certain 'hours, and this by the custom of the country. An attempt has been made by this Bill to limit the number of hours upon government contracts. My hon. friend says why on government contracts alone? The reason has been given by the mover of the Bill when he introduced the Bill and also on the second reading. He expected that this was a principle which would be favoured by legislators and by the people at large but was difficult of realization, and he expected that those who favoured the principle would follow it up, but that it should be commenced by government contracts. That is the only reason I can give to my hon. friend at present. This law is limited to government contracts alone, simply upon the principle that it is expected that the government in this respect will give an example which will be followed by the craft generally. My hon. friend said : Are you not going to create an invidious comparison; do you think you will create a good effect when you have one clas3 of men working for the government who will be compelled to work only eight hours and the others may have to work more than that? I have answered, and I think the mover of the Bill (Mr. Yerville) can confirm me, that in certain cities this very thing is 'already done not by law but by the custom of the trade and that men in cities to-day, in Toronto, Montreal and elsewhere work only for a certain number of hours a day. It may be possible that it would create invidious comparisons but I think it is only a step



in the right direction and that this class of labourers should not be compelled to work more than eight hours a day. We take the first step in this direction and the principle on which it is based is that the working associations themselves have asked it to be limited to that class of labour and to that class alone. That is the only principle of the Bill as I understand it.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: My right hon. friend says that we have limited this to government contracts. My hon. friend has not read the Bill or if he has he has not grasped its sense. He is not now supporting a piece of legislation which stands un the principle that on all government contracts the eight-hour day shall be the rule, but that is the argument that my right hon. friend used. He said that in this we make a commencement. And where do we make a commencement? On government contracts? But my right hon. friend does not make a commencement on government contracts, he picks out one kind of work and one kind of work alone, government contracts on public buildings, and excludes every other. On what principle does my right hon. friend exclude every other? Not on the principle of different classes of work which he was trying to bring to the notice of the House, not at all. Here you have a carpenter at work on a bridge and another carpenter at work on a public building, exactly the same class of work.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: I do not consider that the expression a public ^building would apply in the sense indicated by my hon. friend. A bridge would be a public building.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Then where is the interpretation clause? I do not think that any one would say that a canal was a public building, that a bridge over a canal was a public building, or anything of that kind. It is limited to public buildings, and we quite well know what a public building is. Here is your carpenter, he works on a public building, and he has the eight-hour day. There is the same class of man, the carpenter who works upon another kind of government contract, but he is not protected by the eight-hour principle. Now, does my right hon, friend argue that this is going to apply to all kinds of government work, no matter what, or does he argue that a public building means a public bridge?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: I will take the restricted sense of my hon. friend and say that it applies only to a public building, to a house such as this. Very well. If the men are satisfied for whose benefit this legislation is proposed, then for my part I am satisfied also.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: The difficulty is that they are not satisfied, as I know.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
I have had a great many communications from labouring men and-trades unions all over the country, declaring that they are in favour of the Bill as originally introduced by the member for Maisonneuve, but they are_ not at all in favour of the amendment which is now proposed. There has been some difference of opinion as to what we are now considering, as to tne respects in which, this Bill differs from the Bill originally introduced, and it might be desirable for a moment to examine the two. The Bill as now proposed is restricted to any contract-
Hereafter made for the erection, remodelling, construction or repair of any public building to which the government of Canada is a party.
As my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) has said, it is confined entirely to contracts of the character mentioned, public buildings. It is true that subsection 2 of section 3 of the amended Bill contains this provision:-
The provisions of this section shall, as respects the hours of labour, apply to work undertaken by the government by day labour.
Now, what did the original Bill propose? The original Bill proposed that it should apply, not only to public buildings, but to all the structures enumerated by section 4 of the proposed Act, and these are as follows :-
Public works, such as post offices, custom houses, armouries, Intercolonial stations, freight sheds or locomotive equipment, wharfs, piers, breakwaters, railroads, canals, dredges, navy yards, arsenals, public buildings and vessels for the use of the government.
(b)	contracts for dredging.
(c)	contracts for uniforms, salary, &c., for the militia or permanent or volunteer forces or Royal Northwest Mounted Police, ordnance, rifles, ammunition, mail bags, paper for government printing offices, and also contracts for printing;
(d)	contracts for clothing required for employees of any department of the government, such as letter carriers, navy, prison guards, &c..
(e)	all contracts which contemplate the performance of labour after their execution;
(f)	all work done on construction premises, whether the property in the thing contracted for is vested originally in the government or passes to it on acceptance as fulfilling specifications laid down in the contract.
So hon. members will see that only a trifling portion of the Bill as originally proposed has been retained in the amendment now put forward by the hen. member fer Maisonneuve, with the assent of the Minister of Labour. But that is not the most important difference after all, because the Bill as originally introduced in section 6 contained this provision:-
Every contract to which the government of Canada is a party, which may involve the

employment of labourers, workmen or mechanics, shall contain a stipulation that no labourer, workman or mechanic in the employ of the contractor, sub-contractor or other person doing or contracting to do the whole or any part of the work contemplated by the contract, shall be required or permitted to work upon or in connection with the work contracted for, more than eight hours in any one calendar day except in case of extraordinary emergency.
How is that principle dealt with in the amendment now proposed? The very important elause. ' or permitted,' is left out altogether, and the Bill at present simply provides this:-
Every contract hereafter made for the erection, remodelling, construction or repair of any public building to which the government of Canada is a party, which may involve the employment of labourers, workmen or mechanics, shall contain a stipulation that no labourer, workman or mechanic in the employ of a contractor, sub-contractor or other person doing or contracting to do the whole or any part of the work contemplated by the contract, shall be required, except in case of extraordinary emergency, to work upon Sr in connection with the work contracted for, more than forty-eight hours in any one week or, where employment is for a less time than one week, eight hours in any one calendar day. Additional hours, if worked, shall be classified as overtime and paid for at a rate of not less than time and a quarter.
So the Bill as now proposed is absolutely a different Bill from that which was introduced in the first instance. The whole sphere of its application has been practically reduced to a minimum. Then, instead of the stipulation that no one would be required or permitted to work more than eight hours a day, we have simply a stipulation that no working man shall be required to work more than eight hours a day, leaving it absolutely open as a matter of contract between the employer and the labouring man. He may work ten, twelve or fifteen hours a day as circumstances may render it expedient or necessary. I am not going to argue that point, I merely endeavour to make it clear to the members of this committee that this is an absolutely different proposition from that which was before the committee when the Bill was originally proposed.
Now I would like to say to the Minister of Labour, and to the right hon. gentleman who has spoken upon the subject, that the considerations that were put forth with great force,, and cogency, and eloquence by the Minister of Labour when we were in committee before, do not seem to justify any such divergence from the original scope of the Bill. What did the Minister of Labour say on the first occasion?
If we stop to consider what is the life of the average workingman, we will see how allimportant it is that every one who has at 49i	.
heqrt the welfare of humanity should use what little influence he may have, whether in connection with the government or out of it, to help bring about a condition of affairs which, in the course of time, will bring to every man, whether working on a farm or in a workshop, a condition that will permit him to do eight hours' work, and have part of the balance of the day for enjoyment, and for the necessary development of his faculties, one way or another.
Well, if that be a good principle, and one to which my hon. friend the. Minister of. Labour was willing to commit himself, why does he desire to deny an opportunity for the_ reasonable exercise of his faculties, their reasonable development, and a reasonable enjoyment, to the man who is working upon a wharf, or pier, or breakwater, or railroad, or canal, or dredge, or navy yard, or arsenal? Why should he restrict it entirely to men employed on public buildings? Then he went on further:
Take the case of a workingman working eight or ten hours a day. Supposing he starts work at seven o'clock in the morning, he must rise at five, for workingmen have to start their own fires, to afcist their wives to prepare their own breakfasts, so that five o'clock is as late as any man who is going to work at seven can afford to rise.
Why are not all these considerations so eloquently put forward by the Minister of Labour, applicable to the man who is working upon wharfs, or piers, or breakwaters, or railways or canals, or dredges, or navy yards, or arsenals? That is the problem that presents itself to my mind at the moment, and it is one as to which I hope we may have an answer from the Minister of Labour. He continues as follows:
He leaves his home before seven o'clock, having seen nothing of his children.
Why is not the man who is working upon a pier entitled to see his children before he leaves his home? Is the man who happens to be engaged upon a breakwater to be denied all access to his family while the man who works upon an ordinary public building is to have some such opportunity? Then he went on further:
He works from 7 until 12, which is 5 hours He goes back to his home, he has one hour for rest in the middle of the day, part of which is lost going to and from his work. Sometimes he does not even get that. Sometimes he is obliged to take his dinner can and eat his cold meal at the workshop, and can see nothing of his home during that hour.
Why are not all these considerations cogent with respect to the man who works upon a pier or breakwater? Why should they be . simply taken into consideration in connection with the man who works upon an ordinary public building?
Then he is obliged to work again from one to six o'clock; and if he is to have eight

hours' sleep, which is the least he requires after a hard day's labour, that leaves him only from six to nine to enjoy the comforts of his home. It was never intended by the Creator that the great mass of men should live in that way.
Yet my hon. friend is perfectly willing that a man who works upon a pier or a railway or canal or a wharf or a breakwater should live in that way although he is in the employ of the government, while apparently he has some consideration for the feelings and interests of the man who works upon an ordinary public building. The hon. minister continues :
It was intended that every man should do his share of work and have opportunity to partake of legitimate enjoyment and develop the latent powers and talents with which he is endowed by nature. The working classes have as much love for their families, as great regard for domestic happiness as the rich. They also require a little enjoyment now and then.
I would respectfully point out to my hon. friend the Minister of Labour that the man who works upon pier or breakwater, a railroad, navy yard or arsenal, has feelings and desires with respect to all these matters just the same as a man who works upon an ordinary public building. But, it does seem to me that some reason should be given for restricting the scope of this Bill other than that which has been advanced by the hon. member for Maison-neuve (Mr.- Verville) or even by the right hon. Prime Minister. The Bill as originally introduced had at least some principle behind it. The amended Bill that is presented to us to-day has behind it or in it absolutely no shred or scintilla of any principle whatever.

subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: It seems to me that^ if my hon. friend will pardon me for saying so it has been rather unfortunate, with respect to a most important measure in which a large section of the people have a very deep interest, that my hon. friend should attempt to make party capital out of the Bill which is now before the House.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
I am serious in that and my hon. friend will see on reflection that he has not given to this committee the slightest intimation as to whether he is in
"Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
favour of an eight hour Bill, which would involve all the different contracts which the government might make or whether he is opposed to it. I, myself, would have liked very much to have had my hon. friend's view with regard to the general question. Now, I may say, that I am in favour of the principle that is involved in what is known as the eight hour Bill, but, in considering as to what legislation should be enacted, we must have some regard to the conditions in the country and we must have regard to what may be the general opinion of the people of the country. It is quite true, as my hon. friend has said, that in the Bill as it was originally introduced it did apply to some other things, to-
Contracts for the erection, remodelling, construction or repair of all public works, such as post offices, custom houses, armouries, Intercolonial stations, freight sheds or locomotive equipment, wharfs, piers, breakwaters, railroads, canals, dredges, navy yards, arsenals, public buildings and vessels for the use of the government.
Also to
Contracts for dredging.
And many other things. The Bill, as proposed to he 'amended iby the motion 01 the hon. member who has introduced it, does apply to all public buildings. Therefore, it will include post offices, custom houses, armouries, Intercolonial stations, freight sheds and all public buildings with respect to the building of which the government is a party. It is going a very considerable distance in the direction which the labour organizations of the country desire. They are not getting all they want at the present time, but if this Bill passes it will be the recognition by parliament of a most important principle. It will be the recognition by parliament of the fact that it is desirable to establish an eight-hour day for the labourers engaged upon public works. In that respect I think a very great advance will be made and a very great point will be gained in the interest of the labouring people of the country. If it is found that the application of this principle to public buildings works well, then, at a later session of parliament, we can very well extend the principle to other public works and parliament might very well consider Whether it might not be desirable to make additional provisions such -as were contained in the Bill that the hon. member first introduced. My hon. friend Mr. Borden (Halifax) asks why the Bill does not a/pply to work upon wharfs and 'breakwaters. I can see a difference between work upon breakwaters and wharfs and work upon public buildings. The most important public buildings, indeed, I think all of them, which are erected by the government are in cities or towns. We do not erect public buildings in country districts

and therefore in the great majority of eases we are employing work in localities where, in some eases at all events, the eight hour principle prevails by custom or by arrangement between the contractors and the labouring people.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: It is really an unnecessary provision.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: In some cases it is unnecessary because in a great many cities contracts now provide only for an eight-hour day. But, with respect to wharfs, it is different. Many wharfs are erected in country districts. In many cases the contractor takes his crew of men, goes from place to place where he has contracts for wharfs, camps out, his men live in tents and he carries on his work of constructing the wharfs.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: The minister says that wharfs are built in country places. I understand that they are built in the water.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: If my hon. friend has never seen water in a country place then I pity him.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman forgets that they build them down in Quebec where there is no water.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: I am not aware of that. I am aware that in Quebec when the Conservative government was in power they built a wharf that is now used for a bridge. But, I am not aware that in recent years any wharf has been built where there is no water and where there is no navigation.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: What about the Disraeli wharf?

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: My hon. friend has frequently spoken of the Disraeli wharf, but I have assured myself that my hon. friend is simply imagining things in regard to the Disraeli wharf.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: How many vessels come in there?

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: My hon. friend is diverging from the Bill which is before the committee.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Does my hon. friend realize when he is speaking of building wharfs in country districts that all the labour as a rule is drawn from the city districts?

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: No, that is not the case.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: I beg your pardon; it is the case.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
That is not the case in my own experience. When wharfs are built in the country the labour is drawn from the country districts. The work on the
wharf goes on in the long days of the summer, and unless the men get to work pretty early in the morning and work pretty late hours in the evening they are idle. In many cases they have no opportunity of being with their families.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Away from the cities; away from their families.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
That is one reason why it may not be desirable to legislate with respect to work upon wharfs at the present time at all events, or until we have had some experience in the working of the Bill. Then, with regard to contracts for dredging;
I gave the matter consideration when the Bill was originally introduced, and I have in my mind places where at the present time men upon government dredges work nine hours per day. Upon the contract dredges they work in many cases eleven hours a day. The dredge goes out upon Monday morning after it has taken in its coal and water and does not return to the town near its work until Saturday night. If the hours of the men upon the dredge were limited to eight per day the result would be that early in the morning, and in the evening also, the men would have nothing to do, and they could not be with their families, there would not be the same argument with respect to them as to men engaged on public buildings, and therefore I think it would not be desirable at present to make this Bill applicable to men engaged upon either government dredges or contract dredges. If my hon. friends were to take up other public works they will see that there will be some distinction, perhaps not a wide distinction, but some distinction drawn between work of that character and work upon public buildings. At all events, it does seem to me that it is far better for the labouring people to have this Bill, amended as it is, than to have no Bill at all. I can see how there might be very serious objection on the part of many people to such a broad measure as that first introduced. If this Bill passes it will apply to many of the most important works in which the government is engaged, and with respect to these the government will have adopted the eight-hour principle. That will be a great point gained, and later on if this wins public approval the principle of the measure can be extended to other government works.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Will you extend it to dredging later on?

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
That will be a fair matter for consideration later on. The hon. gentleman from Toronto is of course aware that this parliament would possibly not have the power to interfere as between private contractors and the men they employ, but at all events we are moving in a safe direction now because

we are limiting it solely to public works. It seems to me we are favouring the adoption of a most important principle which will prove of great benefit to the labouring people of Canada. In all probability it will meet with public approval, and it will not be many years before the eight hour principle will be adopted throughout the Dominion not' only with regard to government contracts but to private contracts as well.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: The hon. the leader of the opposition has devoted a good deal of time to showing the difference between the Bill as introduced and the present Bill, but I fear that unwittingly he hardly did full justice to the new Bill. He pointed out that the original Bill stipulated that no labourer or mechanic or workman on these public works should be required ' or permitted ' to work on them more than eight hours a day, and the hon. gentleman said that the dropping of the words ' or permitted ' would leave it open to a contractor to have his men work ten or fifteen hours a day as conditions might require. If the new Bill did anything of the kind it would be open to criticism, but the hon. gentleman will see that there is a provision that if additional hours are worked the additional hours shall be classified as overtime and paid for at the rate of not less than time and a quarter.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: I read it that-

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: I am prepared to admit that, but he did not emphasize that difference when he was pointing out the difference as between the. two clauses. He spoke only of a man working 10 hours or 15 hours but did not say that in that connection it would have to be at the option of the man himself and that if he did work overtime he would get extra pay for the additional hours of work.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Is that all the Bill means, that the man gets quarter time extra?

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: The Bill in this particular follows the custom which labour organizations themselves have adopted. As possibly some members know a good many of these unions have contracts with contractors in which an eight-hour day is fixed. Where such a day has been established there is usually a provision that if longer time is worked it shall be paid for as overtime at an extra rate. Nowhere in the constitution of any trades union that I know of in this country are the words ' or permitted ' used. The unions say that the men shall not be required to work overtime but they make a stipulation whereby if a man works over eight hours he gets payment for overtime. They do not go so far as to say he shall not be permitted to work over eight hours.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: This Bill said that when first introduced.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Exactly and that feature has been omitted evidently because it was not thought wise to go further in endeavouring to regulate a contract between the government and those who were working for it than working men themselves had sought to go in the arrangements they had made as trade unions with their employers. In other words what the hon. member (Mr. Verville) has attempted to do in this clause is to follow the principles which the trades unions themselves have laid down and to endeavour to bring about in regard to government work a condition similar to what some of the larger unions have already succeeded in bringing about in regard to the establishment of this eight hours a day and of payment for overtime at an extra rate when more than that time is worked.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Is the minister aware that overtime is generally paid for at the rate of time and a half and not at time and a quarter.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Yes, I am fully aware of that fact and the probability is that the trades unions themselves will see to it that whenever they can enforce it they will get time and a half or sometimes time and three-quarters.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Why not put it in the Bill?

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
For the simple reason which has governed all through, that this being a new principle, and that the hon. member being anxious to make sure of its adoption, has carefully refrained from going any length to which an exception can be rightly taken. The hon. gentleman says why not put this in the Bill. The hon. the leader of the opposition says:	Why not include
dredging, printing contracts, arsenals, etc., etc.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: I beg pardon, I simply said you included these in the first instance and then dropped them and gave no reason.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: I am glad to know from the hon. member that he was not suggesting that they should be included because his words were calculated to give that impression to the public.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: I am not suggesting that they should or should not be included at the moment, but I say they have been omitted from the Bill as originally suggested, which did have some principle behind it and up to the present time no reason has been given for omitting them.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
The reason is simply that
the inclusion of all these different kinds of

labour in a Bill of this kind would lead to the defeat of the measure in the House.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Why?

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: For the simple reason that one member after the other would bring up small exceptions with particular features and point out the many possible ramifications of so broad a measure and show that the hon. member in endeavouring to introduce a reform had tried to garb everything at once instead of being content with introducing a principle having one thing done for certain and leaving it to time to show whether that would work out advantageously and if so, add other features as time goes on. The policy which gentleman opposite are adopting in trying to make out that the hon. member, by limiting his Bill in certain directions, is not going far enough is simply embarrassing him in the matter of getting through something which would serve as a beginning if they are sincere about the larger measure, they should be willing to support the hon. member to the extent to which he is prepared to go.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Does the hon. minister mean to say that if they are sincere they must be inconsistent? That is what his argument amounts to.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Is there one single line or syllable of this Bill that could not be enforced by order in council? Not one. The government can do this tomorrow without any statute whatever; by order in council, they can enforce every thing in this Bill.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: What about the $200 penalty?

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
Then this Bill is introduced for the sake of the 4th section -the penalty? Now we have the true explanation of it. The government, on every public work in Canada, not only those enumerated in this Bill, but those enumerated in it as first introduced, can by order in council put this principle into effect without coming to parliament at all, and therefore, if they are sincere in their desire for an eight-hour day they have it in their power to give an eight-hour day to every man in Canada employed by the government.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER, Is that the reason my hon. friend is opposed to the Bill?

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: I am not opposing the Bill.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: My hon. friend is not supporting it.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
I am support, ing the principle of the Bill as originally introduced, but not this * Bill, which has
absolutely no shadow of principle behind it The Prime Minister knows that, and so does the Minister of Public Works.

maintopic: NOTICE OF QUESTIONS TO BE INTRODUCED BY MR. MACLEAN (YORK).
subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
In the old Bill, clause 8 provided that the man working eight hours should get the per diem wages, that is, the wages for ten hours' work. _ I think that is the intention of the Bill, From the present Bill that clause has been eliminated, so that if a man goes to a contractor to get work, the contractor will say to him: 'You do not have to work more than eight hours a day unless you like; you may if you choose work 10 hours; I am paying three dollars a day to those who work 10 hours.' If the man does not choose to work 10 hours a day, he gets no work on that contract. I want to know from the minister what follows. Suppose $3 is the regular 10 hr. current wages. If a man works only eight hours a day, the contractor has a right to pay the man only $2.40 a day, or a deduction of 2 hours. There is nothing in this Bill to make him pay more, unless the provision at the end of the Bill for one-fourth more than regular pay for overtime. It is intended to make the working man believe that this measure is in his favour, but it is not so unless it is distinctly provided that if he works eight hours he will get 10 hours' pay.
Progress reported.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext: What business will be taken up to-morrow?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext: We shall take up all the Bills with the exception of the Banking Act and the Bill with regard to the Waterways Treaty.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext: Under the rule, Thursdays are assigned to private members. This year the first Thursday was assumed by a function and another was a religious holiday, so that only two Thursdays were left to private members. I think the intention is that four Thursdays shall be given to private members. The Prime Minister must realize that there are a great many Bills and other matters on the paper that we must dispose of, and it is hardly fair that private members should be limited to two Thursdays, as is the case this year.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I do not know how that is. The rule is that for the first four weeks Thursday shall be private members' day. I think everty- Bill on the Order Paper has been called twice.
House adjourned at six o'clock.



Thursday, January 12, 1911.
